section_summary: This section documents State, War, and Navy Department efforts from 1934 through 1936 to collect and coordinate intelligence on Japanese commercial penetration, immigration, propaganda, espionage, fishing, surveying, and possible military activity around the Panama Canal and throughout Latin America. It includes broad intelligence assessments, requests for diplomatic reporting, naval and military memoranda, press commentary, and reports about the fishing vessel Minato Maru. Later material from 1937-1938 concerns alleged Japanese settlements in Mexico, warnings from Guatemala and Honduras, and Colombian investigations of Japanese mining, petroleum, agricultural, and colonization projects.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on War Department requests for reporting on Japanese activity
subfiles.about: Reports a War Department request that American diplomatic and consular officers collect information on Japanese activity near the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: General Smith says the War Department received alarming reports on Japanese activities in Central America and northern South America, and sought economic and political reports from nine countries.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on coordinating reports of Japanese activities near the Canal Zone
subfiles.about: Clarifies Governor Schley's concern and discusses coordination of Japanese-activity intelligence among the State, War, and Navy Departments.
subfiles.summary: Governor Schley explained that his complaint concerned the failure of military departments in Washington to share and evaluate reports, rather than any failure by diplomatic officers to report. Wilson and General Smith discussed supplying significant State Department reports to M.I.D. and O.N.I., welcoming liaison visits, and considering a coordinating board.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Major Coulter
subfiles.about: Records Military Intelligence Division priorities for reporting Japanese activity, especially in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Major Coulter identified Japanese infiltration, military and naval movements, and espionage as M.I.D.'s principal concerns and asked for renewed reporting from Colombia. The participants agreed on a Colombian instruction, confidential sharing with Governor Schley, and periodic informal conferences.

subfiles.title: Digest of M.I.D. report on Japanese activities in Central and South America
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Military Intelligence Division assessment of expanding Japanese trade and suspected espionage in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum emphasizes rapidly increasing Japanese exports and commercial representation, particularly in Panama. It repeats an attaché's allegation that Panama contained an effective Japanese espionage organization capable of sabotage and argues that commercial penetration often carried political implications.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing sheet for Japanese-activity material
subfiles.about: A fragmentary internal routing or cover page associated with the following secret intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: Routing sheet with largely illegible annotation, apparently routing a Panama-area intelligence report within State.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Adjutant General transmitting a Panama intelligence summary
subfiles.from: Secretary of War, through Alfred T. Smith
subfiles.about: Directs preparation and secure transmission of a secret summary of Japanese infiltration around Panama.
subfiles.summary: Memo orders two copies of a secret summary of Japanese activity through November 1934 sent to the Panama Canal Department commander; supplemental reports to follow.

subfiles.title: Japanese Infiltration in Panama and Vicinity
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese economic, immigration, propaganda, political, and espionage activity in Panama and neighboring Latin American countries.
subfiles.summary: The report describes rapidly growing Japanese trade, immigration, and political contacts in Panama, Costa Rica, Colombia, Peru, Venezuela, and El Salvador. It compiles allegations about hydrographic observation, espionage, prospective sabotage, petroleum and fertilizer acquisition, arms sales, colonies near strategic ports, and possible submarine bases. Many claims are explicitly identified as rumors, secondhand observations, or uncorroborated intelligence.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 198 transmitting a sealed War Department envelope
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Antonio C. Gonzalez, American Minister in Panama
subfiles.about: Requests safe delivery of a sealed War Department envelope to the Panama Canal Department commander.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 198 forwards a sealed War Department envelope for the Panama Canal Department commander, for secure delivery by the Minister.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting information from Colombia, Venezuela, and Peru
subfiles.about: Requests State Department assistance in gathering military-relevant information from three countries near the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: Burnett explains that budget restrictions prevent stationing military attachés in Colombia, Venezuela, or Peru, despite their potential use as bases for unfriendly activity. He asks diplomatic and consular personnel to provide the information described in an attached outline and to report emergencies rapidly through the American Minister in Panama.

subfiles.title: Expansion of Military Intelligence Activities in the Vicinity of the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Lists political, economic, military, naval, espionage, and propaganda information desired from Venezuela, Colombia, and Peru.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum defines detailed collection requirements concerning Japanese influence, trade missions, strategic raw materials, aviation, shipping, armed forces, coastal defenses, budgets, arms purchases, and naval establishments. It gives particular emphasis to espionage and propaganda affecting the Panama Canal Zone and adjacent areas.

subfiles.title: Letter establishing State Department reporting arrangements with M.I.D.
subfiles.about: Confirms a trial arrangement for sharing Japanese-activity reports with the Military Intelligence Division.
subfiles.summary: Wilson says relevant despatches from Central America, Colombia, Venezuela and Peru will go to M.I.D., whose officer will periodically review summaries and reports.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on conference with Majors Coulter and Almond
subfiles.about: Records agreement on reporting procedures and possible reassignment of a military attaché to Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Majors Coulter and Almond accept the report-sharing mechanism, clarify Brabson's list is guidance, and discuss moving an attaché to Colombia.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 560: Delivery of Sealed Envelope
subfiles.about: Confirms personal delivery of the sealed War Department envelope to Major General H. B. Fiske.
subfiles.summary: Burdett acknowledges receipt of Instruction No. 198 and reports that a commissioned legation officer personally delivered the envelope. Pages 30 and 31 are duplicate true copies of the same despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 943: Japanese Activities in South America
subfiles.about: Reports a Russian minister's claims about Japanese submarine bases and warship sales in South America.
subfiles.summary: The Russian Minister alleged that Japanese agents sought submarine bases and fuel-oil supplies in Peru, Venezuela, and northern Brazil for operations aimed at the Panama Canal. He also claimed that Peru had ordered thirty-five Japanese warships and suggested Brazil might have placed a similar order, but offered no further sourcing.

subfiles.title: Report of an alleged Japanese espionage appropriation
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Relays a European minister's report that Japan had appropriated funds for espionage in Central and South America.
subfiles.summary: Source claims Wakabayashi said Japan's Foreign Office allotted 5,500,000 yen for Latin American espionage in 1934 and created a Cultural Office to run it.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence transmittal of Fifteenth Naval District report
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential naval intelligence report from Balboa for State Department information and filing.
subfiles.summary: Puleston forwards the Fifteenth Naval District commandant's April 8, 1935 letter; the cover adds nothing.

subfiles.title: Intelligence Items of Particular Interest
subfiles.from: W. S. Crosley, Commandant, Fifteenth Naval District
subfiles.to: Chief of Naval Operations, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Reports on alleged Japanese espionage funding, commercial propaganda, the British naval mission to Colombia, and American aviators there.
subfiles.summary: The report repeats the allegation that Wakabayashi described a large Foreign Ministry espionage appropriation but finds little direct evidence of military propaganda, espionage, or sabotage around Panama. It also assesses the British naval mission to Colombia and explains why American aviators employed during the Leticia conflict were leaving Colombian service.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Fifteenth Naval District report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the April 8 confidential naval intelligence report.
subfiles.summary: Wilson thanks Puleston for transmitting the Fifteenth Naval District commandant's letter. The document is a brief administrative acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Guatemala despatch on Bauer Avilés
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a Guatemala despatch discussing Bauer Avilés's comments on American anxiety over Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Guatemalan despatch on press commentary about Japanese activity in Central America (Bauer Aviles).

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 786: Editorial Comment Regarding Japanese Activities
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Guatemalan editorial about Japanese economic expansion and its strategic implications.
subfiles.summary: Bauer Avilés argued that Japanese commercial agreements in Central America might acquire political and strategic significance and that changing American defense policy reflected growing concern about Japan. He considered stronger Canal Zone air defenses prudent but warned Central American governments that agreements with Japan could bring American pressure or retaliation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for report on a Japanese military mission
subfiles.about: References a military attaché report concerning a Japanese military mission visiting South American countries.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Report No. 5190 from the military attaché in Argentina on a Japanese military mission.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence transmittal concerning Japanese fishing activities
subfiles.about: Forwards an Eleventh Naval District report and enclosure on Japanese fishing in Central American waters.
subfiles.summary: Puleston sends Duggan a copy of the commandant's report concerning Japanese fishing operations. The letter identifies the material as restricted.

subfiles.title: Japanese Fishing Activities—Central America
subfiles.from: W. T. Tarrant, Commandant, Eleventh Naval District
subfiles.to: Chief of Naval Operations, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese plans for large trawlers operating from San Pedro and in Mexican and Central American waters.
subfiles.summary: Report: Japan plans to freeze fish for canneries or shipment through Manzanillo or Panama; the Navy first opposed operations near the US, then withdrew objection as relations improved.

subfiles.title: Press clippings on Japanese fishing and unidentified submarines
subfiles.from: Los Angeles Japanese Daily News and Los Angeles Times
subfiles.about: Reports the Minato Maru fishing venture and an unidentified submarine group near the Galápagos Islands.
subfiles.summary: Clippings: reported Japanese fishing rights near the Panama Canal, the Minato Maru's departure for Mexico, and unconfirmed submarines near San Cristobal Island.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of report on Japanese fishing activities
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the Eleventh Naval District material on Japanese fishing.
subfiles.summary: Duggan thanks Puleston for transmitting the November 5 report and enclosure. The letter is an administrative acknowledgment without additional analysis.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for War Department request on Japanese espionage
subfiles.about: References a War Department request for cooperation in collecting information on Japanese espionage around the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a War Department request for State assistance in collecting intelligence on Japanese espionage in Central America and parts of South America.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence letter transmitting notes on the Minato Maru
subfiles.about: Transmits notes concerning the activities of the Japanese fishing vessel Minato Maru.
subfiles.summary: Puleston tells Hornbeck the enclosed notes on the Minato Maru may interest him.

subfiles.title: Notes on Minato Maru
subfiles.about: Describes the vessel, crew, equipment, surveying, government contacts, and suspicions surrounding the Minato Maru.
subfiles.summary: Notes on the Minato Maru: disciplined crew, well-equipped vessel and extensive shallow-water surveying from Panama to the Gulf of California fed suspicions of government or navy links, even narcotics; circumstantial and contested.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 166: Editorial on Japanese Espionage
subfiles.about: Transmits a Honduran editorial warning about Japanese espionage and Wakabayashi's Central American travels.
subfiles.summary: Erwin encloses an El Cronista editorial drawing on Diario de Costa Rica reports about alleged Japanese espionage around Panama. The editorial urges Honduras to exercise caution in dealing with Wakabayashi and other visiting Japanese agents.

subfiles.title: El Cronista editorial: Espionaje japonés
subfiles.about: A Spanish-language editorial portrays Japanese immigration and commerce as instruments of future military expansion and espionage.
subfiles.summary: El Cronista editorial links Japan's China war to alleged penetration of the Americas through trade, immigration and fishing; cites Canal surveillance and Wakabayashi, urging caution toward Japanese agents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Colombian despatch on Japanese encroachment
subfiles.about: References Winthrop Greene's despatch on Colombian opposition to Japanese encroachment and Japanese interest in Venezuelan petroleum.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Colombian despatch: the government is determined to prevent unwanted Japanese activity; information on Japanese residents and Venezuelan petroleum interests.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2147 on Japanese interests in Colombia
subfiles.about: Reports Colombian surveillance of Japanese engineers, intercepted diplomatic communications, and official resistance to Japanese encroachment.
subfiles.summary: Greene describes secret-service monitoring of Shiro Ohmachi and Hiroji Takahashi and encloses reports on their exploration of lands near the San Juan River, the Corinto colony, and Joseph T. Boyd. Colombian authorities also intercepted messages between Minoda and Ogimi concerning Ono Tadao's pursuit of Venezuelan petroleum and prospective commercial exchange. Greene concludes that senior Colombian officials opposed Japanese encroachment and would act to prevent it.

subfiles.title: Translated Colombian report on Japanese activities near the San Juan River
subfiles.about: Investigates Japanese engineers studying the Miller lands for mining, agriculture, petroleum, and possible colonization.
subfiles.summary: Colombian report: Japanese engineers surveyed the San Juan River area with Bylander and Boyd for gold, oil and crops, reportedly contemplating a 5,000-person colony; the agent saw it as strategically sensitive.

subfiles.title: Translated memorandum on the Japanese colony at Corinto
subfiles.about: Describes an established Japanese agricultural settlement near Corinto in Cauca.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: about thirty Japanese families at Corinto farm kidney beans in organized shared-equipment farms; low living standard, profitable, no strategic danger.

subfiles.title: Supplementary translated report concerning Joseph T. Boyd
subfiles.about: Adds information on Boyd's negotiations with Japanese interests and related petroleum exploration in Venezuela.
subfiles.summary: Boyd confirms a wealthy Japanese firm seriously considered San Juan lands for agriculture and petroleum, and sent two engineers to Venezuela; notes his Guapi River concession.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum asking whether to reply or file
subfiles.about: Asks whether the attached communication from Guatemala should receive a reply or merely be filed.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt refers the Des Portes material to the Under Secretary, asking for a recommendation on replying.

subfiles.title: Letter on President Ubico's concern about Japanese activity
subfiles.about: Reports President Ubico's concern about Japanese settlement and fishing activity and recommends an investigation.
subfiles.summary: Ubico told Des Portes more than 100,000 Japanese were in Mexico and fishing vessels worked from Panama through Mexico; Des Portes recommends L. A. McIntire investigate.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese colonies in Mexico
subfiles.about: Records claims that very large groups of undocumented Japanese men had settled in Baja California and along Mexico's Pacific coast.
subfiles.summary: Des Portes records rumors that Japanese settlers in Mexico were trained soldiers; two sources estimated 150,000-200,000 undocumented men, unverified; continues beyond this section.
